html:
The Apalachee were a Muskogean-speaking people of the Florida Panhandle, between the Aucilla and Ochlockonee rivers around today's Tallahassee. They were rich maize farmers living in towns with mounds, one of the late Mississippian chiefdoms.

The Narváez expedition passed through in 1528, and Hernando de Soto spent the winter of 1539 to 1540 in their main town, Anhaica. From 1633 Spanish Franciscans built missions among them, and Apalachee maize fed Spanish St Augustine and Havana. In 1704 English Carolinians and their Creek allies destroyed the missions and killed or enslaved thousands. The survivors scattered to Pensacola, Mobile and later Louisiana, where an Apalachee community still lives. Their neighbours were the Timucua. See also Apalachees.
